$$
P(X<x)=P(Z<\frac{x-\mu }{\sigma })
$$

where $Z∼N(0,1)$ is a standard normal random variable. In our case, we have $\mu =-4$ and $\sigma =1.$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<-4.47) & =P(Z<\frac{-4.47-(-4)}{1}) \\  & =P(Z<-0.47) \\  & =P(Z\le -0.47) \\  & =Φ(-0.47)\end{aligned}
$$

The required probability is represented by the area shown below.

According to the table, we have

$$
Φ(-0.47)=0.3192.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
P(X<-4.47)=0.3192.
$$

Given a normal random variable $Y∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),$ we have

$$
P(Y\ge y)=P(Z\ge \frac{y-\mu }{\sigma })
$$

where $Z∼N(0,1)$ is a standard normal random variable. In our case, we have $\mu =-2$ and $\sigma =4.$

First, we transform $Y$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y\ge -4.48) & =P(Z\ge \frac{-4.48-(-2)}{4}) \\  & =P(Z\ge -0.62).\end{aligned}
$$

The required probability is represented by the area shown below.

$$

$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z\ge -0.62) & =1-Φ(-0.62) \\  & =1-0.2676 \\  & =0.7324.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$

Example: 
                    Computing the Probability of a Normal Random Variable on an Unbounded Interval
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Given a normal random variable $X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2),$ we have

$$
P(X <       x) = P \left( Z <       \dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma} \right)
$$

where $Z \sim N(0,1)$ is a standard normal random variable. In our case, we have $\mu = 2$ and $\sigma = 2.$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<1.24) & =P(Z<\frac{1.24-2}{2}) \\  & =P(Z<-0.38) \\  & =P(Z\le -0.38) \\  & =Φ(-0.38)\end{aligned}
$$

The required probability is represented by the area shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14263116/assets/48d92806543cb86b2906032b1723fa942db842e7f283681cafeeb9b11fca8cab.png)

According to the table, we have

$$
\Phi(-0.38) = 0.3520.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
P(X <               1.24) = 0.3520.
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Computing the Probability of a Normal Random Variable on an Unbounded Interval Using the Complement
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Given a normal random variable $Y \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2),$ we have

$$
P(Y \geq y) = P \left( Z \geq \dfrac{y-\mu}{\sigma} \right)
$$

where $Z \sim N(0,1)$ is a standard normal random variable. In our case, we have $\mu = 5$ and $\sigma = 4.$

First, we transform $Y$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y\ge 2.92) & =P(Z\ge \frac{2.92-5}{4}) \\  & =P(Z\ge -0.52)\end{aligned}
$$

The required probability is represented by the area shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14263116/assets/049e4733082674668ebbe2c5a710cd847f1db16d26fdcd2af6e603941efdffe7.png)

Now, we express the required probability in terms of $\Phi(z)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z\ge -0.52) & =1-P(Z<-0.52) \\  & =1-P(Z\le -0.52) \\  & =1-Φ(-0.52)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we know that

$$
\Phi(-0.52) =0.3015.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z\ge -0.52) & =1-Φ(-0.52) \\  & =1-0.3015 \\  & =0.6985.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
P(Y \geq 2.92) = 0.6985.
$$

                    Computing the Probability of a Normal Random Variable on a Bounded Interval
canonical_examples.problem:
The data below is taken from the table of values of the cumulative distribution function $\Phi(z)$ for the standard normal distribution. Given that $X \sim N(1,9),$ compute $P(-1.13 < X < 3.25).$
$z$$\, 0.00 \,$$\, 0.01 \,$$\, 0.02 \,$
$\, -0.9 \,$ $\, 0.1841 \,$ $\, 0.1814 \,$ $\, 0.1788 \,$
$\, -0.8 \,$ $\, 0.2119 \,$ $\, 0.2090 \,$ $\, 0.2061 \,$
$\, -0.7 \,$ $\, 0.2420 \,$ $\, 0.2389 \,$ $\, 0.2358 \,$
$z$$\, 0.03 \,$$\, 0.04 \,$$\, 0.05 \,$
$\, 0.5 \,$ $\, 0.7019 \,$ $\, 0.7054 \,$ $\, 0.7088 \,$
$\, 0.6 \,$ $\, 0.7357 \,$ $\, 0.7389 \,$ $\, 0.7422 \,$
$\, 0.7 \,$ $\, 0.7673 \,$ $\, 0.7704 \,$ $\, 0.7734 \,$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Given a normal random variable $X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2),$ we have

$$
P(a <        X <        b) = P \left( \dfrac{a-\mu}{\sigma} <        Z <        \dfrac{b-\mu}{\sigma} \right)
$$

where $Z \sim N(0,1)$ is a standard normal random variable. In our case, we have $\mu = 1$ and $\sigma = \sqrt 9 = 3.$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-1.13<X<3.25) & =P(\frac{-1.13-1}{3}<Z<\frac{3.25-1}{3}) \\  & =P(-0.71<Z<0.75)\end{aligned}
$$

The required probability is represented by the area shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14263116/assets/a50513f550d8a3122e2f2276883a0189fe9bdc6dd19159e8ae94dbd5b247f5a9.png)

Now, we express the required probability in terms of $\Phi(z)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-0.71<Z<0.75) & =P(Z<0.75)-P(Z\le -0.71) \\  & =P(Z\le 0.75)-P(Z\le -0.71) \\  & =Φ(0.75)-Φ(-0.71)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.71) & =0.2389 \\ Φ(0.75) & =0.7734\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-0.71<Z<0.75) & =Φ(0.75)-Φ(-0.71) \\  & =0.7734-0.2389 \\  & =0.5345.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
P(-1.13<          X <          3.25) = 0.5345.
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
The **normal distribution** has the probability density function

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{x-\mu}{\sigma} \right)^2},
$$

where the $\mu$ represents the mean and $\sigma$ represents the standard deviation. To state that $X$ follows a normal distribution, we write $X \sim N(\mu,\sigma^2).$

The graph of this probability density function forms a bell curve centered at $x=\mu.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14263116/assets/c9359fc84401aabb19e526755b70647cb0496fa8ddba65974466e0ffc3dbbbdc.png)

In general, the greater the standard deviation $\sigma,$ the flatter the bell curve. Intuitively, this makes sense because the standard deviation represents how "spread out" the distribution is.

tutorials.name: Transforming a Normal Random Variable into a Standard Normal Random Variable
tutorials.problem:
To compute a probability involving a normally distributed variable $X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2),$ it is convenient to transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
Z = \dfrac{X - \mu}{\sigma}
$$

So, we have

$$
P(X <  x) = P \left( Z <  \dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma} \right)
$$

where $Z \sim N(0,1)$ is a standard normal random variable.

For example, suppose we have a random variable $X \sim N(1,2^2)$ and we want to compute $P(X \leq 1.4)$ using the following $z$-table: 

| $z$ | $\, 0 \,$ | $\, 0.01 \,$ | $\, 0.02 \,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\, 0 \,$ | $\, 0.5 \,$ | $\, 0.504 \,$ | $\, 0.508 \,$ |
| $\, 0.1 \,$ | $\, 0.5398 \,$ | $\, 0.5438 \,$ | $\, 0.5478 \,$ |
| $\, 0.2 \,$ | $\, 0.5793 \,$ | $\, 0.5832 \,$ | $\, 0.5871 \,$ |

The $z$-table above shows the cumulative probabilities for a normal random variable $Z \sim N(0,1).$ In order to use the table to compute $P(X \leq 1.4),$ we must first transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 1.4) & =P(Z\le \frac{1.4-1}{2}) \\  & =P(Z\le 0.2)\end{aligned}
$$

According to the table, we have

$$
P(Z \leq 0.2) = 0.5793 .
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(X \leq 1.4) = 0.5793.
$$
